notes.definition: The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants. Burning fuels can release carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen, as well as solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons that form particulates.
explanation: The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants. Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may also contain some sulfur. The gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned may include carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may also be released, forming particulates in the atmosphere.

With plenty of oxygen, complete combustion happens: the carbon in the fuel is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen to water. For methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). When the oxygen supply is limited, incomplete combustion happens. Some carbon is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide (CO), for example 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l), and some is not oxidised at all, forming soot, which is solid carbon particles: CH₄(g) + O₂(g) → C(s) + 2H₂O(l).

Sulfur dioxide is produced when fuels that contain sulfur as an impurity are burned. The sulfur reacts with oxygen: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g). Coal and some crude oil fractions contain sulfur, so power stations and ships burning these fuels can release sulfur dioxide.

Oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ, mainly NO and NO₂) are produced when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the high temperatures in engines and furnaces. The nitrogen does not come from the fuel. For example N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), and then 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g).

You should be able to predict the products of combustion from the composition of the fuel and the conditions. If the fuel contains carbon, expect carbon dioxide (or carbon monoxide and soot if oxygen is limited). If it contains hydrogen, expect water. If it contains sulfur, expect sulfur dioxide. If combustion happens at a very high temperature in air, expect oxides of nitrogen. A fuel that is pure hydrogen produces only water: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), although oxides of nitrogen can still form if it burns in air at high temperature.
keyFacts: Combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
Most fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may contain some sulfur.
Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen) gives carbon dioxide and water.
Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) gives carbon monoxide and/or soot (carbon particles), plus water.
Sulfur dioxide forms when sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen: S + O₂ → SO₂.
Oxides of nitrogen form when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperatures, for example in engines.
Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates.
Hydrogen as a fuel produces only water (but NOₓ may form at high temperature in air).

keyTerms.definition: A substance released into the environment that can cause harm.
Burning with plenty of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water from a hydrocarbon.
Burning with a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
Tiny solid particles (such as soot) and unburned hydrocarbons released into the atmosphere.
Gases such as NO and NO₂ formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperatures.
SO₂, a gas formed when sulfur impurities in fuels are burned.

workedExamples.title: Predicting the products of combustion
workedExamples.question: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a car engine where the oxygen supply is limited and the temperature is very high. Predict the products.
steps: Carbon: limited oxygen, so carbon monoxide and soot (carbon particles) as well as some carbon dioxide.
High temperature in air: nitrogen and oxygen react to give oxides of nitrogen.
Unburned hydrocarbons may also be released.
workedExamples.answer: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, soot (particulates), water vapour, sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburned hydrocarbons.

workedExamples.title: Balancing an incomplete combustion equation
workedExamples.question: Balance the equation for the incomplete combustion of propane to carbon monoxide and water: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO + H₂O.
steps: Oxygen on the right: 3 + 4 = 7 atoms, so 3.5 O₂; double everything to remove the half.

workedExamples.title: Mass of sulfur dioxide from coal
workedExamples.question: A power station burns 1000 kg of coal containing 2.0% sulfur by mass. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced. S + O₂ → SO₂. Ar: S = 32, O = 16.
steps: 1 mol S gives 1 mol SO₂, so mass SO₂ = 20 × 64 ÷ 32 = 40 kg.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think oxides of nitrogen come from nitrogen in the fuel.
misconceptions.right: In fact they form when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperatures in engines and furnaces.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sulfur dioxide comes from all fuels.
misconceptions.right: In fact it only forms when the fuel contains sulfur as an impurity, for example coal.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think incomplete combustion produces no carbon dioxide at all.
misconceptions.right: In fact it often produces a mixture of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and soot, depending on how limited the oxygen is.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hydrogen-fuelled vehicles produce carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact hydrogen contains no carbon, so burning it produces only water, although NOₓ can form at high temperatures.

realWorld: Car exhausts are fitted with catalytic converters to reduce emissions of carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen.
Many power stations use flue gas desulfurisation to remove sulfur dioxide before gases are released; road fuels in the UK have most sulfur removed.
Gas boilers and fires must be serviced to make sure they have enough air supply so that incomplete combustion does not produce carbon monoxide.
examTips: Link each pollutant to its cause: CO and soot from limited oxygen; SO₂ from sulfur in the fuel; NOₓ from nitrogen and oxygen in the air at high temperature.
Do not say NOₓ comes from the fuel; say 'nitrogen from the air'.
When predicting products, look at the elements in the fuel and the conditions (amount of oxygen, temperature).
Check that combustion equations balance, especially the oxygen atoms; it can help to balance C, then H, then O.
summary: Burning fuels is a major source of pollutants.
Complete combustion: carbon dioxide and water.
Incomplete combustion: carbon monoxide and soot.
High temperatures in engines produce oxides of nitrogen from air.
Soot and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates.

questions.question: Which pollutant is produced when fuels burn with a limited supply of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Limited oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide. Sulfur dioxide comes from sulfur in the fuel.

questions.question: What is soot?
questions.explanation: Soot is carbon that has not been oxidised, produced in incomplete combustion.

options: the fuel contains sulfur as an impurity

questions.question: Where does the nitrogen in oxides of nitrogen from a car engine come from?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen in air react at the high temperatures in the engine. Petrol is a hydrocarbon and contains essentially no nitrogen.

questions.question: Which is the balanced equation for the formation of sulfur dioxide?
questions.explanation: One sulfur atom and one O₂ molecule give one SO₂ molecule. Oxygen exists as O₂ molecules.

questions.question: Which is the balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of methane to carbon monoxide and water?
questions.explanation: Check: C 2 = 2, H 8 = 8, O 6 = 2 + 4. The second option has 4 O on the left but only 3 on the right.

questions.question: A fuel contains only carbon and hydrogen. It is burned in plenty of air at a very high temperature. Which list contains all the expected products?
options: Carbon dioxide, water and oxides of nitrogen
Carbon monoxide, soot and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide, water and oxides of nitrogen
questions.explanation: Plenty of air means complete combustion (CO₂ and H₂O). The high temperature allows N₂ and O₂ from the air to form NOₓ. No sulfur is present, so no SO₂.

questions.question: A vehicle runs on hydrogen fuel burned in air in an engine. Which pollutant could still be produced?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen contains no carbon, so no carbon-based pollutants form. But the high temperature in air can still produce NOₓ.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of sulfur dioxide, SO₂.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): S = 32   O = 16
questions.explanation: One sulfur atom (32) plus two oxygen atoms (2 × 16 = 32) gives 64.

questions.question:
A power station burns 1000 kg of coal containing 2.0% sulfur by mass.
All of the sulfur reacts to form sulfur dioxide.
S + O₂ → SO₂
Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): S = 32   O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of sulfur = 2.0% of 1000 kg = 20 kg
1 mark: Mr SO₂ = 64; 1 S gives 1 SO₂
questions.explanation: The mass doubles because each sulfur atom (32) gains two oxygen atoms (32) to form SO₂ (64).

questions.question:
Methane can undergo incomplete combustion to produce carbon monoxide.
2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O
Calculate the mass of carbon monoxide produced when 32 g of methane undergoes incomplete combustion.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1   O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio CH₄ : CO = 2 : 2, so 2 mol CO
questions.explanation: Mr of CH₄ = 16 and of CO = 28. Moles of CO equal moles of CH₄, so 2 × 28 = 56 g.

questions.question: Name two gases produced when a hydrocarbon fuel burns completely.
questions.explanation: Complete combustion oxidises all the carbon and hydrogen.

questions.question: Give the formula of carbon monoxide.
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide has one carbon atom and one oxygen atom. Do not confuse it with Co (cobalt) or CO₂.

questions.question: Describe how carbon monoxide and soot are produced when fuels burn.
markScheme: 1 mark: incomplete combustion / limited supply of oxygen
1 mark: carbon in the fuel is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide, or not oxidised at all, giving carbon particles (soot)
questions.explanation: Both come from carbon in the fuel when there is not enough oxygen to make carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Describe how oxides of nitrogen are produced in a car engine.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrogen and oxygen from the air react
1 mark: at the high temperature in the engine
questions.explanation: Petrol does not supply the nitrogen. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO at high temperature.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for sulfur burning in oxygen.
questions.explanation: Sulfur is a solid; oxygen and sulfur dioxide are gases.

questions.question:
Balance this equation for the formation of soot by incomplete combustion of propane:
C₃H₈ + O₂ → C + H₂O
questions.explanation: Carbon: 3 C. Hydrogen: 8 H gives 4H₂O. Oxygen: 4 O on the right, so 2O₂. Check: C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 4 = 4.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the composition by mass of a diesel fuel.
Predict the pollutants released when the diesel burns in a lorry engine.
Give the reason for each.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon monoxide and/or soot (particulates) because of incomplete combustion / limited oxygen
1 mark: sulfur dioxide because the fuel contains sulfur
1 mark: oxides of nitrogen because nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperature in the engine
questions.explanation: Predict from the elements in the fuel and from the conditions in the engine.

questions.question: Suggest two ways to reduce the amount of carbon monoxide produced by a gas boiler.
markScheme: 1 mark: make sure there is a good supply of air/oxygen (ventilation)
1 mark: regular servicing so the burner works correctly and combustion is complete
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion, so the key is enough oxygen.

questions.question: Which of these, released when fuels burn, form particulates in the atmosphere?
options: Solid particles (such as soot) and unburned hydrocarbons
markScheme: 1 mark: solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons
questions.explanation: Particulates are tiny solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons. The other options are gases.

questions.question: Name the element present as an impurity in coal that produces sulfur dioxide when the coal burns.
questions.explanation: Sulfur in the fuel reacts with oxygen to form sulfur dioxide. Note the AQA spelling 'sulfur'.

questions.question: Describe how burning fossil fuels produces carbon monoxide, soot, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.
markScheme: Indicative content: fuels contain carbon and hydrogen, and may contain some sulfur; carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited; soot (carbon particles) also from incomplete combustion; sulfur dioxide from sulfur impurities reacting with oxygen, S + O₂ → SO₂; oxides of nitrogen from nitrogen and oxygen in the air reacting at high temperatures in engines.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct origin of at least three of the four pollutants described.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two pollutants linked to a correct cause.
questions.explanation: Each pollutant has a different cause; be precise about which comes from the fuel and which from the air.

questions.question:
A student compares two fuels, A and B.
Table 1 shows information about the fuels.
Predict and explain the products of combustion for each fuel.
Include balanced equations where you can.

rows: mainly carbon, with some hydrogen and 2% sulfur
in a power station furnace at a very high temperature

markScheme: Indicative content: Fuel A: plenty of oxygen so complete combustion, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; products carbon dioxide and water vapour; no sulfur so no SO₂; little CO or soot; some NOₓ possible if flame very hot. Fuel B: carbon gives CO₂ (C + O₂ → CO₂); some incomplete combustion may give CO and soot (particulates); hydrogen gives water; sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, S + O₂ → SO₂; very high temperature in air gives oxides of nitrogen, N₂ + O₂ → 2NO; ash and unburned material form particulates. Comparison: Fuel B releases more pollutants.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): products for both fuels correctly predicted and explained in terms of composition and conditions, with at least two correct balanced equations.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): products for both fuels mostly correct with some explanation, or one fuel explained in detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct products named with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use a systematic approach: elements in the fuel, oxygen supply, and temperature.
